## Robustness of STRUCTURE / ADMIXTURE

[STRUCTURE](https://web.stanford.edu/group/pritchardlab/structure.html),
[ADMIXTURE](https://dalexander.github.io/admixture/), and other genetic
clustering methods are extremely popular across the field of population
genomics. However, it has been shown that very different models can produce
exactly the same STRUCTURE / ADMIXTURE clustering patterns (see [Figure 2 in
that study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-05257-7/figures/2), and
an [accompanying
post](https://www.molecularecologist.com/2016/08/05/on-misinterpreting-structureadmixture-results/)
on this paper). As a result, we have to be quite careful with the interpretation
of the results.

**Here are a few suggestions on what you could do in this study depending on
your level of familiarity and prior experience:**

### 1. Have you used one of these genetic clustering methods?

**Write a _slendr_ model corresponding to the demographic history you've
inferred, then try to experiment with its parameters or topological structure in
a way following the approach the authors took in this study. How robust is your
inference when you repeat it on these simulated models?**

### 2. Are you thinking about using one of these genetic clustering methods?

**Write a simulation script for each of the three model topologies in the figure
linked above. Follow the methodology of the paper and try to replicate their
results, including modifying the three models to convince yourself of the
conclusions.**

### Tip: How to convert data

Note that _slendr_ doesn't produce PLINK files yet, but we do have `ts_vcf()`
and `ts_eigenstrat()` conversion functions (see
[this](haplotype-methods.html#exercise-converting-tree-sequences-to-other-genotype-formats)
exercise from our workshop for a quick overview). You can use these functions to
produce outputs from your simulations converted from the original tree sequence,
then do the necessary PLINK conversion to be able to run ADMIXTURE or STRUCTURE.
